The development is carried out by modifying the calculation of Value at Risk (VaR) to consider the skewness and kurtosis values (hereinafter referred to as modified VaR), so that the Keywords: normal distribution assumption can be eliminated. As a method for compiling a stock Modified value at risk; portfolio, the Multi-Objective Optimization technique was chosen because it can modify Multi-objective optimization; risk averse so that the risk can be adjusted to the risk profile of each investor and is able Portfolio risk analysis; to stabilize the mean return value. For its implementation, this paper uses real stock data Risk averse; which of course has returns that are not normally distributed, namely the four Indonesian Stock portfolio. stocks based on the largest capitalization recorded in January 2025 (blue chip), namely BREN, BBCA, BYAN, and BBRI obtained through finance.yahoo.com. The analysis method is divided into three steps, including multi-objective optimization completion, portfolio return calculation, and finally modified VaR estimation. The results of the study show that BBCA has the largest weight with a portion of more than 40% of the four stocks, so BBCA will be the priority stock for this portfolio. The portfolio formed using multi- objective optimization is proven to have a stable mean return because the portfolio mean return is between several of its constituent stocks (vice versa) which is around 0.01%, and the smallest estimated value of the portfolio modified VaR is 1.67%. Thus, a portfolio based on multi-objective optimization is not only able to create a portfolio that provides a small risk in risk measurement without assuming a normal distribution, but at the same time multi-objective optimization is also able to provide competitive returns with its constituent stocks. MODIFIED STATISTICAL-BASED VALUE AT RISK FOR MULTI-OBJECTIVE OPTIMAL-BASED… 1. INTRODUCTION Investment is one way to develop assets owned to get profits in the future. In general, investment can be made in various forms, both real asset investment and financial asset investment [1]. In addition, based on the objectives, investment can also be divided into two categories, namely short-term investment and long- term investment [2]. Investment goals often influence decision making. The decisions taken are used to maximize the profits that will be obtained [3]. Investments that guarantee high profits are stocks. Stocks with stable returns and little amounts of liabilities are targets that are always sought by investors [4]. Stocks that have these characteristics are referred to as blue chip stocks [5]. This type of stock is usually stocks that are well known on the Stock Exchange because they have products that have become market leaders [6]. Although blue chip stocks have stable profits, they also have high investment risks [7]. Investment risk is a condition where investors fail to get their capital because the issuer of shares is declared bankrupt, or the shares are not sold on the Stock Exchange [8]. To minimize investment risk, investors can form an optimal portfolio by using diversification. A portfolio is defined as a collection of stocks or securities with a certain level of return and risk. Portfolio risk analysis is usually faced with the abnormality of the distribution of returns on the constituent assets, so that the risk measures obtained may not be appropriate. The portfolio is made as efficient as possible, which can provide the greatest possible expected return value with minimal risk. [9]. There are several methods to form an optimal portfolio. Those forms are maximizing profits, minimizing volatility, targeting profits, targeting volatility, or maximizing profits and minimizing volatility. The greater the volatility of each investment, the greater the possibility of profit or loss [10]. Value at Risk (VaR) is a metric commonly used in statistical disciplines to measure the maximum risk of loss on a value movement with a certain level of confidence [11]. The variance-covariance method and the historical simulation method are the most frequently used approaches in the Value at Risk method [12]. In the variance-covariance method, it is assumed that the volatility of an investment return or portfolio is normally distributed. While the historical simulation method is assumed that the return from an investment or portfolio is not normally distributed [13]. However, VaR is basically developed under the assumption of normal distribution, thus requiring the data or returns analyzed to be normally distributed. On the other hand, real return data almost always does not follow a normal distribution. Therefore, it is necessary to develop its statistical distribution so that it can be more flexible and not bound by the necessity of assuming a normal distribution. In related research, Gunjan and Bhattacharyya generally provide a review related to portfolio optimization, one of which is based on value at risk [14]. Next, Zhou conducted research in optimizing portfolios for financial data with a mean-variance approach, which was then analyzed for risk using conditional value at risk [15]. In addition, multi-object-based optimization can also be used to make optimal stock portfolios [16]. This paper uses the Multi-Objective Optimization technique in stock portfolio optimization. Next, it proposes the development of a statistical distribution in risk analysis based on Value at Risk that does not require the assumption of a normal distribution. For its real implementation, this paper applies it to analyze the risk of a portfolio of several Indonesian stocks. The Indonesian Stock Portfolio used comes from leading stocks. Meanwhile, the order of the remaining parts of this paper is arranged as follows. In the second part, we propose a literature review including Indonesian Blue-Chip Stocks, Portfolio, Multi-Objective Optimization, and Value at Risk. The next section, methodology used in this research, includes data, completion of multi-objective optimization, calculating portfolio returns, and VaR estimation. Next, the main section presents the results and some discussion details. At the end of the paper, it is closed to a conclusion. 2. Based on market capitalization, stocks are divided into three types, namely blue-chip, middle-tier, and small-chips shares. The difference is that blue-chip shares have a market capitalization value of above ten trillion, medium-cap shares have a market capitalization value of between one trillion to five trillion, and small-chip shares have a market capitalization value of under 1 trillion [17]. Second, the proposed development of a VaR-based risk measurement method to ignore the assumption of normality of returns provides a successful measurement showing the smallest estimated modified VaR value of the stock portfolio, which is 1.67%. Thus, it can be concluded that Multi-Objective Optimization can not only create a portfolio that provides a small risk, but at the same time, Multi-Objective Optimization can also provide competitive returns with its constituent stocks. In addition, the proposed development of modified VaR has successfully provided a calculation of risk value without requiring the assumption of normality distribution to be met. Basically, this study is limited to avoiding the assumption of normality so that it does not pay attention to the distribution of returns. For future research, development can be carried out by modifying the VaR formula so that it can be specifically applied to one or several specific distributions, which can better guarantee the risk measure obtained is able to describe the actual investment risk value. JSON: Name: modified_var_multiobjective_portfolio Title: Integration of Cornish–Fisher modified Value-at-Risk into a multi-objective mean–variance portfolio optimization for non-normal Indonesian stock returns Short Hypothesis: Integrating a Cornish–Fisher modified Value-at-Risk estimator that incorporates sample skewness and kurtosis into a multi-objective mean–variance portfolio optimization produces portfolios with statistically significantly lower 95% daily VaR than portfolios produced by standard variance-covariance optimization or historical-VaR-optimized portfolios on the same non-normal Indonesian blue‐chip return series. Related Work: Existing portfolio construction methods center on mean–variance optimization and its extensions; traditional variance-covariance approaches assume normal returns and use sample covariance for risk, which underestimates tail risk when returns are skewed or leptokurtic. Historical-simulation VaR avoids normality assumptions but is sensitive to limited historical extremes and can systematically under- or over-estimate tail quantiles. Cornish–Fisher and other moment-adjusted approximations extend parametric VaR to include skewness and kurtosis but are approximations that can be unstable for extreme higher moments. Conditional approaches (GARCH-EVT) model tail behavior explicitly but require heavy modeling and tuning and are computationally more complex. Multi-objective and weighted-objective portfolio formulations allow explicit trade-offs between return and risk-aversion but are typically paired with standard variance or CVaR risk metrics. Limitations across current methods include reliance on normality or large-sample historical extremes, sensitivity to moment and covariance estimation noise, lack of a simple pipeline combining moment-adjusted VaR with multi-objective weight selection, and limited out-of-sample backtesting focused on non-normal emerging-market equities. Abstract: This work addresses portfolio risk measurement and construction when asset returns deviate from normality. We propose a pipeline that integrates a Cornish–Fisher moment-adjusted Value-at-Risk estimator (incorporating sample skewness and kurtosis) into a multi-objective mean–variance optimization framework parameterized by a risk-aversion index. Portfolio weights are obtained from a closed-form Lagrangian solution with explicit risk-aversion control; tail risk is subsequently estimated via the modified VaR rather than the standard normal approximation. The main contribution is a reproducible, end-to-end procedure that produces investor-specific allocations while producing VaR estimates that account for non-normal return features. We expect the method to yield portfolios with lower empirical tail losses at fixed confidence levels while maintaining competitive mean-return profiles compared with variance-based and historical-VaR benchmarks. The pipeline is designed for daily return series from emerging-market blue-chip equities but is applicable to other non-normal asset sets. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = daily closing prices for PT Barito Renewables (BREN), PT Bank Central Asia (BBCA), PT Bayan Resources (BYAN), PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia (BBRI), 2023-10-09 to 2025-02-25; secondary datasets = (a) extended Indonesian blue-chip universe (top 20 by market cap) same period, (b) synthetic return series with controlled skewness/kurtosis and varying tail behavior generated from skewed-t and mixed-normal mixtures. Baselines: (1) Markowitz mean–variance optimization with parametric normal VaR (variance-covariance), (2) portfolio weights from mean–variance optimized then risk measured by historical-simulation VaR, (3) CVaR-constrained optimization (expected shortfall minimization), (4) GARCH-filtered returns + EVT tail VaR. Evaluation metrics: daily VaR at 95% and 99%, Expected Shortfall (ES) at 95% and 99%, mean return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, number and rate of VaR breaches, Kupiec Proportion of Failures test, Christoffersen independence test, rolling out-of-sample cumulative loss, and turnover. Experimental setup: compute log returns; test normality per instrument and portfolio (Kolmogorov–Smirnov); estimate sample mean, covariance, skewness, kurtosis; compute closed-form multi-objective weights for a grid of risk-aversion mu ∈ {100, 250, 500, 1000, 2500}; compute modified VaR using Cornish–Fisher per portfolio and per instrument; perform walk-forward backtest with in-sample window = 250 trading days, out-of-sample window = 60 days, rolling step = 20 days; record metrics per out-of-sample window; compute bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 resamples) for VaR and ES. Ablations and comparisons: (A) Cornish–Fisher modified VaR vs parametric normal VaR using identical weights; (B) multi-objective weighting vs single-objective (variance-only, return-only) using modified VaR measurement; (C) sensitivity to estimation window length (125, 250, 500 days) and covariance shrinkage; (D) compare performance on synthetic series to test behavior under controlled skewness/kurtosis. Statistical analysis: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of out-of-sample VaR and ES between proposed pipeline and each baseline, report p-values and effect sizes. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cornish–Fisher approximation accuracy deteriorates for extreme skewness/kurtosis and may produce unreliable quantiles under heavy tails or multimodal distributions. 2) Moment estimates (skewness, kurtosis, covariance) are noisy in small samples, producing unstable weights and VaR estimates. 3) The approach retains VaR's known limitation of not being a coherent risk measure and not capturing tail loss severity beyond the quantile; it may prefer portfolios with similar VaR but worse tail losses. 4) Results can be sensitive to the choice of risk-aversion parameter mu and the in-sample estimation window; tuning can overfit historical idiosyncrasies. 5) Backtesting on a limited set of blue‐chip Indonesian stocks and a finite period limits external validity and generalization to other markets or regimes. 6) Transaction costs, liquidity constraints, and market impact are not modeled and may invalidate real-world performance. 7) Covariance matrix inversion and estimation can be ill-conditioned for larger universes, limiting scalability without regularization. 8) The pipeline assumes temporal stationarity within estimation windows; structural breaks will degrade performance.
